Dear Reviewers and ACs,

Thank you once again for your time and effort in reviewing our paper and for providing insightful, constructive feedback. We would like to take this opportunity to briefly summarize our work and formally conclude the author-reviewer discussion.

Our paper introduces $\textbf{DetectiumFire}$, the first large-scale, multi-modal dataset for fire understanding. From the initial review, we received supportive feedback from all reviewers, each of whom acknowledged the value of the proposed dataset. We are especially grateful to Reviewer BhUn for recognizing the improvements made in the paper compared to previous versions and for providing constructive feedback.

During the rebuttal period, we submitted detailed responses, additional dataset documentation and annotation quality metrics, as well as further experiments on VLM reasoning and video modeling. We also appreciate Reviewer zWe7’s important point regarding dataset scale. While we acknowledge that DetectiumFire is smaller than some general-purpose datasets, it offers high-quality annotations, broad fire-type diversity, and strong real-world utility. We believe it already enables meaningful benchmarking for tasks such as object detection, synthetic data generation, and VLM reasoning. Although we cannot alter the dataset for this submission, we are committed to iterative updates to expand its scale and diversity in future releases.

Overall, we sincerely thank all reviewers and the ACs for their thoughtful engagement and valuable feedback throughout the review process. We are pleased to have addressed most concerns, and these discussions have significantly strengthened our paper.

Sincerely,

Authors of Submission 1041

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below we address the remaining concerns: 

1) Annotation Quality and Inter-Annotator Agreement

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the lack of detailed annotation quality metrics in the current submission. Below, we provide additional information about our annotation guidelines and quality control processes to clarify this aspect.

Our annotation pipeline is structured around three key tasks:

1.	Bounding box annotation of fire regions in the images

2.	Caption generation: Creating 75-token descriptive captions covering what is burning, where it is burning, and its severity (no/low/moderate/high risk)

3.	Preference annotation: Selecting preferred images between pairs of synthetic samples generated by different diffusion models and justifying the choice based on general preference, visual appeal, and prompt alignment

All annotators are affiliated with a startup focused on reducing industrial fire-related risks through digital twinning and AI technologies (the company name is omitted to maintain anonymity in double-blind review). Annotators either possess prior fire-related domain experience or have participated in related projects and are familiar with basic computer vision concepts.

During annotation, each annotator will be allocated one batch of data. To ensure quality, any ambiguities or disagreements during annotation are recorded and discussed with the technical officers. Once an annotator completes a batch of data, it is automatically routed for review. Each annotation is checked, and a minimum 90% agreement rate is required for batch approval. This includes:

•	Bounding box accuracy

•	Caption accuracy (coverage of key fire scene elements)

•	Preference validity based on the established criteria (general preference, visual appeal, and prompt alignment
)

We chose the 90% threshold acknowledging that 100% agreement is neither practical nor necessarily desirable, as it may introduce reviewer bias. If a batch falls short of this threshold, the technical officer and the annotator jointly discuss the issues, and the data is re-annotated.

Tools Used:

•	For bounding boxes, we used the Roboflow platform, which supports annotation task assignment, collaborative batch review, and merging.

•	For caption and preference annotation, we built a lightweight custom annotation tool (see Appendix C.3). This tool manages batch allocation and allows technical officers to review JSON outputs visually. We plan to release our custom annotation tool to support similar efforts in fire-related or multi-modal data annotation.


2) Caption Length and Expressiveness

We appreciate the concern about the 75-token caption limit. As discussed in Section 3.1,  constraints were adopted to balance prompt richness and diffusion model quality, as excessively long captions often introduce irrelevant details that degrade generation performance.  These short prompts focus on core attributes: what is burning, where, and severity, which are essential for generating visually grounded, fire-specific images.

We agree that the current prompt format may limit expressiveness for advanced reasoning tasks. As part of our ongoing dataset development, we are actively exploring a \textbf{second-tier annotation layer} with longer, context-rich captions. These will not replace but \textbf{complement} the current prompts: the short captions remain optimized for synthetic image generation and lightweight VLM training, while the second-tier annotations will support more nuanced tasks such as causal reasoning, fire progression modeling, and structured scene reporting.

In fact, as noted in Appendix C.2, we have already begun to explore structured metadata such as human presence and condition. We plan to expand this layer in future releases to further enhance VLM capabilities in high-stakes, safety-critical applications.

3) Utility of Synthetic Data

We agree that synthetic-only training underperforms real data, as shown in Table 3. However, our results serve as a baseline to demonstrate the minimal performance achievable using synthetic data alone. Notably, even this baseline outperforms models trained on the D-Fire dataset, a real-world dataset with over 5k fire images, achieving 59.40% mAP@50 (SFT) and 58.08% (RLHF) on DetectiumFire compared to 48.04% for the D-Fire-trained model (Table 2). This highlights that our synthetic data, despite its limitations, provides meaningful signal and transferability.

We acknowledge that current synthetic generation techniques are not yet a substitute for real-world diversity and nuance. However, we view this as a promising foundation for future research. The DetectiumFire synthetic set offers a well-structured benchmark upon which future advances in data generation, e.g., simulation-based methods, GANs, or enhanced diffusion pipelines, can be evaluated. One long-term goal is to reach or exceed real-data performance using scalable synthetic pipelines.

Furthermore, as we discussed in the response to Reviewer zWe7 (regarding dataset size constraints), many high-quality fire images and videos, especially from industrial or sensitive domains, are unavailable due to privacy and licensing restrictions. These are often proprietary or confidential, making public release impossible. In contrast, synthetic data can be freely distributed and even used in commercial settings, providing a viable and scalable alternative in scenarios where real data is restricted.

4) Limited Video Modeling

We acknowledge that our initial TimeSformer-based video classification baseline is relatively simple and may not fully exploit the temporal modeling capabilities required for nuanced fire scene understanding. Our primary focus was on the release and documentation of the DetectiumFire dataset, for which a basic and interpretable baseline was preferred.

To further explore more advanced architectures, we evaluate the recent VideoMamba model [1], a structured state space model (SSM)-based video backbone designed as an efficient alternative to transformers for video understanding. Specifically, we fine-tune three variants of VideoMamba: Ti, S, and M, on our dataset using a single A100 GPU with a batch size of 4. We vary the number of frames (8, 16) and follow the default training hyperparameters from the official VideoMamba implementation. The dataset is split into 70% training, 20% validation, and 10% test, consistent with the setting used for TimeSformer (see Appendix E.1), to ensure fair comparison. The results are as follows:

| Model         | Pretraining | Resolution | #Frame | Top-1(%) |
|---------------|-------------|------------|--------|-------|
| VideoMamba-Ti | ImageNet-1k | 224        | 8x3x4  |  81.35     |
| VideoMamba-Ti | ImageNet-1k | 224        | 16x3x4 | 83.13      |
| VideoMamba-S  | ImageNet-1k | 224        | 8x3x4  |   84.93   |
| VideoMamba-S  | ImageNet-1k | 224        | 16x3x4 |   85.27  |
| VideoMamba-M  | ImageNet-1k | 224        | 8x3x4  |   85.16    |
| VideoMamba-M  | ImageNet-1k | 224        | 16x3x4 |   86.04  |

Interestingly, while VideoMamba demonstrates solid performance across different configurations, we observe that it consistently underperforms TimeSformer on our fire dataset, which is not expected given its strong performance on general-purpose video benchmarks. This suggests that VideoMamba may not transfer as effectively to the fire understanding domain. Some potential reasons for this could be: 1) VideoMamba’s state space design excels at modeling smooth and continuous temporal dynamics, which are prevalent in action recognition datasets like Kinetics [2]. However, fire-related events, such as sudden flare-ups, flickering, or rapid spreading, often involve chaotic and non-stationary motion patterns. These may be better captured by transformer-based models that attend flexibly across time. 2) The Mamba architecture is known for its efficiency due to low-rank approximations and memory compression. While this helps scale to long sequences, it may inadvertently discard fine-grained temporal details crucial for fire scene interpretation, such as frame-level intensity shifts or flickering textures.

In summary, these findings highlight the importance of tailoring temporal modeling architectures to the unique characteristics of fire-related video data. Future work may explore hybrid models that combine the efficiency of Mamba with the flexibility of temporal attention techniques to better bridge the gap between general video datasets and fire-specific understanding.

[1] Li, Kunchang, et al. "Videomamba: State space model for efficient video understanding." European conference on computer vision. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024.

[2] Kay, Will, et al. "The kinetics human action video dataset." arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.06950 (2017).

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below we address the remaining concerns: 

1) Short Help Statement Regarding Dataset Code

We appreciate the reviewer’s observation regarding the lack of detailed documentation. In response, we have prepared a comprehensive and user-friendly README.md that thoroughly documents all components of the dataset. This documentation is available on the same Dataset URL we provided.

Specifically, it provides detailed descriptions of the four main components of the dataset:

•	Real-world images (with YOLO annotations and metadata)

•	Real-world videos (fire and non-fire)

•	Synthetic images (generated via supervised fine-tuning and RLHF)

•	Preference dataset (used for RLHF/DPO fine-tuning)

The README also includes metadata format explanations and usage instructions. All data are organized to support direct integration with standard pipelines for:

•	Object detection (e.g., YOLOv11)

•	Diffusion model fine-tuning (SFT and RLHF)

•	Vision-language model training (via prompt-supervised learning)

We believe this addition significantly improves the accessibility and usability of the dataset for both academic and applied research.

2) Dataset Scale is Smaller than Expected.

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the dataset scale. It is true that DetectiumFire is smaller than some general-purpose datasets. Several factors limit raw scale but also reflect the care and intent behind our curation.

•	Collection Challenges:  Real fire scenes, particularly rare or high-risk cases (e.g., industrial incidents), are difficult to safely capture and verify. Footage from these scenarios often comes with strict privacy or licensing restrictions, limiting its redistribution. Although web search serves as an alternative data source, it too is constrained by licensing terms, typically restricting usage to non-commercial research purposes.

•	Annotation Complexity: The absence of reliable pre-trained fire detection models limits the effectiveness of automated tools in filtering fire images or assisting with annotation, particularly for data gathered via web search. As a result, both the filtering and annotation processes in DetectiumFire rely heavily on human validation. While this approach ensures high-quality, accurate labels, it also reduces the speed and scale at which data can be processed.

•	 Avoiding Reduncy: Previous datasets like D-Fire contain large numbers of images extracted from nearly every video frame, resulting in redundancy without added diversity. In contrast, our focus is on $\textbf{long-tail, high-utility coverage}$ rather the scale. We believe this careful curation offers more value for training robust models than sheer volume.

We also recognize the importance of scale and are committed to expanding the dataset over time. Our plans include:

•	Licensing-Safe Expansion: We now prioritize collecting data from web platforms (e.g., YouTube, TikTok) with clear public content policies. Where possible, we will also release videos/images recorded from IoT devices in real fire scenarios.

•	Semi-Automated Annotation: As our object detection and VLM models improve, we are beginning to use them to assist in filtering and annotation, significantly reducing manual workload.

We view this release as a foundational dataset with high-quality annotations, broad fire-type diversity, and real-world utility. We are committed to iterative updates and welcome community feedback to grow DetectiumFire in both scale and impact.

3) Limited Qualitative Analysis in VLM Reasoning

We acknowledge that detailed qualitative analysis can significantly strengthen our experimental evaluation. To address this, we conducted an in-depth per-sample breakdown of correctness across key fire reasoning components. 

First, we analyzed object match and environment match by comparing the outputs of the original model and the SFT fine-tuned model.

•	Object Match: 52.63% of samples were correctly answered by both models, while 34.75% were correctly answered only by the SFT model, and 10.10% only by the original model. Only 2.53% were incorrect in both cases.

•	Environment Match: 62.73% of cases were correct for both models, with 26.67% correct only under SFT and 9.09% only under the original model. Only 1.52% of examples were incorrect in both.

These results demonstrate that the SFT model not only improves aggregate accuracy but also resolves additional cases that the original model fails to handle, supporting our claim that fine-tuning with DetectiumFire yields tangible gains in structured fire-related reasoning.

We further evaluated the models using a 4-class confusion matrix on fire severity prediction. Below are the normalized confusion matrices for both models:

Original Model

Ground Truth ↓ Prediction →  No Risk   Low   Moderate   High  

No Risk      31.6%   6.1%      32.7%   29.6%          

Low Risk    7.0%    47.4%     15.8%     15.8%         

Moderate Risk    2.0%    10.2%     61.2%    28.6 %       

High Risk     6.3%     8.3%       8.3%   81.3%          

SFT Model

Ground Truth ↓ / Prediction →	No Risk	Low	Moderate	High

No Risk	85.1%	8.5%	6.4%	4.3%

Low Risk	1.8%	66.7%	10.5%	7.0%

Moderate Risk	8.2%	10.2%	73.5%	10.2%

High Risk	2.1%	2.1%	12.5%	87.5%

From the above results, we observe:

1.	All severity levels show clear improvements in diagonal accuracy (i.e., correct predictions) with the SFT model.

2.	False alarms are dramatically reduced. For instance, the original model misclassified "No Risk" cases as "High Risk" 30.6% of the time, an unacceptable outcome in safety-critical applications. This is reduced to just 4.3% in the SFT model.

3.	Improved severity alignment illustrates that the SFT model better understands fire context and threat levels.

In addition, we provide detailed examples where the SFT model correctly identifies components of the fire scene that the original model fails to recognize. Due to the constraints, we provide the exact image name in our DetectiumFire dataset.

Image path: msg5430551134-14034_jpg.rf.e907eebddbf0c52fbef71874c2c314b7.jpg

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful, constructive, and encouraging feedback. We are especially grateful that you took the time to compare the current submission with the earlier ICML version and acknowledged the improvements in detail.

Below, we address the remaining concerns in detail: 

1)  Deliberate Use of Established Methods with Future Extensions

We agree that DetectiumFire is primarily positioned as a dataset contribution, and we deliberately adopted widely-used pipelines (SFT and RLHF) to ensure replicability and isolate the dataset’s utility.  We also acknowledge the value of architectural or tooling innovation. In the future version, we plan to elaborate further on the custom annotation GUI we developed (Appendix C.3), which streamlines caption verification and prompt editing for safety-critical domains. We are also exploring releasing it as a lightweight open-source annotation tool for safety-related multimodal datasets.


2) RLHF vs. SFT Results Are Predictable

We appreciate the reviewer’s point that the performance differences between RLHF and SFT follow intuitive expectations.  However, we believe that experimental confirmation of these trends in the fire domain remains non-trivial and valuable, given the limited exploration of preference learning in safety-critical, high-variance visual phenomena like fire.  

On the other hand, the assessment dimensions we adopted (general preference, visual appeal, prompt alignment [1]) were chosen for comparability with prior work, but may be insufficient to capture $\textbf{fire-specific fidelity}$. Unlike well-defined objects such as “cats” or “dogs” commonly used in benchmarks like Pick-a-Pic [2], or MS-COCO [3], fire exhibits high visual entropy: its shape, color, texture, and opacity are dynamic, chaotic, and context-dependent. This introduces unique challenges in both generation and evaluation. For instance, two images may both appear visually appealing but differ drastically in realism if one contains unnatural flame colors or violates plausible fire behavior. Clearly, we did not incorporate any fire-specific criteria in the current fine-tuning or evaluation pipeline. It is entirely possible that when assessed using such fire-aware criteria, which differ dramatically from conventional ones, the relative performance of SFT and RLHF may differ.

As part of future work, we plan to explore the following $\textbf{fire-aware evaluation criteria}$, such as:

•	$\textbf{Flame morphology}$: Does the generated shape and motion trail resemble plausible fire dynamics?

•	$\textbf{Color plausibility}$: Are the color gradients (e.g., yellow-to-orange-to-black smoke) consistent with real fire physics?

•	$\textbf{Contextual correctness}$: Is the flame behavior (size, direction, dispersion) coherent given the surrounding objects or environment?

•	$\textbf{Propagation cues}$: Are there signs of realistic spread patterns or secondary ignition?

Unfortunately, due to time constraints during the rebuttal window, we were unable to annotate and implement these ideas. Nevertheless, we believe our work lays a strong foundation and highlights the need for such specialized metrics in generative evaluation for fire understanding.

[1] Wallace, Bram, et al. "Diffusion model alignment using direct preference optimization." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2024.

[2] Kirstain, Yuval, et al. "Pick-a-pic: An open dataset of user preferences for text-to-image generation." Advances in neural information processing systems 36 (2023): 36652-36663.

[3] Lin, Tsung-Yi, et al. "Microsoft coco: Common objects in context." European conference on computer vision. Cham: Springer International Publishing, 2014.


3) Limited Expressiveness of Captions for Advanced VLM Tasks

We appreciate this insightful observation. As in our earlier submission, we chose to retain concise 75-token captions to balance prompt expressiveness with the synthesis quality of diffusion models, which tend to degrade when faced with lengthy or tangential scene descriptions. These short prompts focus on core attributes: what is burning, where, and severity, which are essential for generating visually grounded, fire-specific images.

We agree that the current prompt format may limit expressiveness for advanced reasoning tasks. As part of our ongoing dataset development, we are actively exploring a $\textbf{second-tier annotation layer}$ with longer, context-rich captions. These will not replace but $\textbf{complement}$ the current prompts: the short captions remain optimized for synthetic image generation and lightweight VLM training, while the second-tier annotations will support more nuanced tasks such as causal reasoning, fire progression modeling, and structured scene reporting.

In fact, as noted in Appendix C.2, we have already begun to explore structured metadata such as human presence and condition. We plan to expand this layer in future releases to further enhance VLM capabilities in high-stakes, safety-critical applications.



Once again, we deeply appreciate your detailed suggestions, especially those carried over from the earlier ICML review cycle. Your insights have been instrumental in improving the quality, transparency and depth of our work, and we are encouraged by your positive assessment!

The most prominent characteristics include diversity of coverage in the real world, encompassing rare categories, indoor/outdoor images/videos, and fires/non-fires. strengths_contributions.value:
- The strongest point is to gather diverse datasets. It is generally acknowledged that confusing data can arise in the fire-detection problem. Therefore, gathering images and videos of fires and non-fires in various environments is very valuable.
- The utility of synthetics is validated. In the fire detection problem, generating synthetics can be a cautious process. This paper provides a very delicate process for this. 
- Combining the LLM and vision can be promising due to the power of LLM. Additionally, LLM-related prompts can offer more detailed reasoning or causal explanations.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The scale of the dataset is somewhat small compared to the expected. 
- In experiments, the VLM’s capability of fire-reasoning is too short because there is no detailed qualitative analysis for the results. For example, a confusion-like table can be helpful to understand the prediction results.

final_justification.value:
Although there are some limitations in size, I can accept the decision made by the reviewers and AC. I'll keep my score.

The dataset consists of raw data and annotations by models, well-curated for long-tail and high utility coverage. The annotation procedure's accuracies look good, and the proposed alg. shows the reasonable accuracy. The qualitative analysis is helpful to understand the performance of the proposed alg. During the rebuttal, the previous points are more clarified and validated. However, my issue is the size, which is required to obtain generalized results over time and across regions. This limitation is evident when the benchmark dataset has a size restriction, as fires exhibit characteristics that are influenced by seasonality.

It makes me hesitant to make a clear decision. However, other merits, such as well-curated, multi-modality, and sound generation steps, make me accept the other reviewers' positive decision.

summary.value:
This paper presents DetectiumFire, a large-scale, multi-modal benchmark dataset designed for fire-related visual understanding and synthetic image generation. The dataset includes over 26,000 images, 2,000 videos, and 12,000 human preference pairs, covering both real and synthetic fire scenarios. Key components include bounding box annotations, risk-level metadata, and prompt-aligned synthetic samples generated via finetuned diffusion models.

The authors benchmark the dataset across various tasks: object detection, anomaly detection, synthetic image evaluation, and video-text alignment. The evaluation includes comparisons with prior datasets (e.g., DFireDataset, FLAME SD), generative baselines (SFT vs RLHF), and ablation on synthetic-vs-real performance. Risk levels and cross-domain coverage (e.g., wildfires, industrial fires) are incorporated to enrich data diversity and realism.

strengths_contributions.value:
1）Compared to earlier versions (e.g., ICML 2025 submission), this paper significantly improves clarity, dataset transparency, and experimental depth. Many concerns from earlier reviews have been directly addressed (see below).

2）The dataset comprises a diverse blend of real-world fire scenarios (wildfire, urban, industrial) and well-curated synthetic content. Captions, prompts, risk-levels, and user preferences enhance its utility for both visual and vision-language tasks.

3）Ethical Transparency and Licensing: Unlike earlier versions, the NeurIPS submission includes detailed licensing information for all external data (Appendix D), ensuring clarity regarding re-use and intellectual property compliance.

4）A key concern raised earlier (lack of explanation on risk-levels) has been addressed. Section 3.4 now details how risk labels (no/low/moderate/high) are assigned, and Table 4 connects these annotations to detection performance.

5）Clearer interpretation of why FLAME SD performs poorly (e.g., synthetic artifacts),
Justification of model anomalies (e.g., Faster-RCNN outperforming YOLOv11), Ablation studies across synthetic/real data combinations.

6）Authors now explain downstream use cases (e.g., emergency simulation, firefighter training, VLM robustness) for multi-modal fire data (Section 1 & 6).

7）Writing is clean, figures (e.g., Fig. 7–9) are informative, and the dataset/code is publicly accessible.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1） The authors rely on well-established finetuning techniques (SFT, RLHF) and standard diffusion models. Though justified as a dataset paper, some architectural or pipeline innovation (e.g., in annotation tooling or data validation) would strengthen technical contributions.

2） RLHF vs. SFT Results Are Predictable: Although Section 5.3 compares both strategies, the findings align with prior knowledge (RLHF performs better in preference alignment). More surprising or counterintuitive findings would strengthen the benchmark’s impact.

3） The use of 75-token captions remains, and while the rationale is explained (Section 3.3), the limited expressiveness may reduce training richness for some VLM tasks.

summary.value: This paper introduces DetectiumFire, a multi-modal dataset for fire understanding tasks. The dataset includes traditional computer vision annotations (bounding boxes) and detailed textual descriptions for each sample. The authors validate their dataset across object detection, synthetic image generation via diffusion models, and vision-language reasoning tasks. They claim DetectiumFire addresses data scarcity in fire detection and enables better performance compared to existing benchmarks like D-Fire.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The dataset is significantly larger than existing fire detection datasets, with both images and videos included. 

2. The multi-modal nature with textual descriptions is genuinely useful for modern AI applications.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. While the paper mentions fire safety experts, there is minimal discussion of inter-annotator agreement, annotation guidelines, or quality metrics beyond basic human review. For a safety-critical domain, this seems inadequate. The 75-token caption limit appears arbitrary and may lose important contextual information.

2. Table 3 clearly shows synthetic-only training performs much worse than real data. The claimed "slight improvement" from real+synthetic is marginal and could be statistical noise. The synthetic data pipeline seems to add complexity without clear benefits.

3. The video experiments are insufficient, relying on basic TimeSformer classification without more sophisticated temporal modeling.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The authors provide detailed experimental settings and claim reproducibility.

final_justification.value: Thanks for the detailed response. The explanation of the annotation quality control process is particularly convincing, and the other clarifications are helpful. I will maintain acceptance of the paper.

title.value: DetectiumFire: A Comprehensive Multi-modal Dataset Bridging Vision and Language for Fire Understanding

abstract.value: Recent advances in multi-modal models have demonstrated strong performance in tasks such as image generation and reasoning. However, applying these models to the fire domain remains challenging due to the lack of publicly available datasets with high-quality fire domain annotations.  To address this gap, we introduce $\textbf{DetectiumFire}$, a large-scale, multi-modal dataset comprising of 22.5k high-resolution fire-related images and 2.5k real-world fire-related videos covering a wide range of fire types, environments, and risk levels. The data are annotated with both traditional computer vision labels (e.g., bounding boxes) and detailed textual prompts describing the scene, enabling applications such as synthetic data generation and fire risk reasoning. DetectiumFire offers clear advantages over existing benchmarks in scale, diversity, and data quality, significantly reducing redundancy and enhancing coverage of real-world scenarios. We validate the utility of DetectiumFire across multiple tasks, including object detection, diffusion-based image generation, and vision-language reasoning. Our results highlight the potential of this dataset to advance fire-related research and support the development of intelligent safety systems. We release DetectiumFire to promote broader exploration of fire understanding in the AI community.
